theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you terminate a cable in a distribution board, what must be done to the board?
options: Switch off the main breaker and start straight away
Ask a colleague to stand by the switch for you
Isolate it, lock off and tag, then prove it dead
Turn off the room lights so you can see any sparks

questions.stem: After you prove a circuit dead, why do you check your voltage tester on a known live source again?
options: To show that it did not fail during the test
To charge its battery for the next job
To reset the reading back to zero
To store the time of the test in its memory

questions.stem: What are the layers of a typical armoured power cable, from the inside out?

Conductor, armour, insulation, sheath, bedding

The cone and clamping ring

questions.stem: When you cut back the armour wires of an armoured cable, what must you avoid?

Cutting part way through each wire, then bending it
Bending the wires back gently before they break off
Cutting into the bedding and the inner insulation

questions.stem: What is the shroud on an armoured cable gland for?

It makes the earth connection to the armour wires

Paper soaked in oil

questions.stem: Why must the end of an MI cable be sealed soon after it is stripped?

So the conductors do not lose their shape
So the gland can be tightened more easily
The powder absorbs moisture from the air

questions.stem: You seal an MI cable end. An insulation resistance reading then falls slowly over a few minutes. What does this suggest?

The tester battery is fully charged

questions.stem: How many twisted pairs are in a standard Cat 6 data cable?

To make the cable stronger to pull in
To make the colours easier to see
To let the cable carry mains power

Each pair untwisted for at least 50 mm or more

questions.stem: What is the usual greatest length of a twisted-pair Ethernet channel, from device to device?

options: It may be carrying mains voltage

Invisible light from it can damage your eyes
The end of the cable may be very hot

Put them in a marked, sealed container

A layer of solder melted over the strands
A wrap of insulating tape on the strands
A crimped bootlace ferrule

Choose the biggest lug in the box to be safe

So the conductor is cut through and held
So the terminal does not need a cover

questions.stem: Screened (shielded) control cable has a foil or braid around the cores. What is the screen for?
options: To make the cable stronger to pull
To carry the neutral current back to the main panel
To protect signals from electrical interference
To keep the cores dry in wet places

questions.stem: Unless the drawing says otherwise, how is the screen of an instrument signal cable usually earthed?
options: At both ends and at every joint
At one end only, to avoid earth loops

questions.stem: Why must the correct size of cable gland be used?

So the gland is cheaper to buy
So the gland matches the colour of the box
So it seals and grips the cable properly

questions.stem: A gland is fitted to an outdoor box. What does a gland with the right seal keep out?
options: Water and dust
Heat and light
Air and sound
Signals and noise

questions.stem: How should you use a cable knife to remove a cable sheath?
options: Cut towards your body for better control
Cut deep in one stroke so the sheath comes off fast
Cut away from your body, not into the cores
Hold the cable on your leg while you cut

questions.stem: Where would you find which core of a control cable goes to which terminal?
options: On the label stuck on the side of the cable drum

On the inside of the tool box lid

To insulate the bare ends of the cores
To stop the cores touching the gland

questions.stem: A thick armoured cable is to be bent into a panel. What should you check?

That you bend it as tight as possible, to save room in the panel
That the cable is heated first to soften it
That the armour is removed at the bend

questions.stem: Why is fire-resistant cable used for a fire alarm circuit?
options: It is cheaper than ordinary cable
It is easier to bend neatly round tight corners
It keeps working for a time in a fire
It does not need any fixings

questions.stem: Which test checks that the insulation between the cores of a new armoured cable is sound?
options: A continuity test
An insulation resistance test
A polarity test
A voltage test using a test lamp

questions.stem: Before an insulation resistance test on a cable, what must be done?
options: The cable is connected to its load and switched on
The cable is made wet so the reading is clear
The tester is set to its lowest ohms range
The cable is isolated and disconnected at both ends

questions.stem: What does a high insulation resistance reading between two cores tell you?
options: The insulation is in good condition
The cores are touching each other
The cable is too long for the circuit
The tester battery is flat

questions.stem: What does a continuity test on a newly terminated core check?
options: That the core is not touching any other core
That the core is unbroken from end to end
That the cable is the right colour
That the insulation is thick enough

questions.stem: After terminating cables, what should be written on the job sheet?
options: The names of the tool suppliers
The weather and the temperature on each day of the work
Cable labels, test results and any problems
The price of each cable gland used

questions.stem: What should you do with cable off-cuts, sheath strips and armour wire at the end of the job?
options: Sort them into the right bins for scrap and waste
Leave them inside the panel enclosure for the next worker
Push them into the cable tray out of sight
Burn them in the yard to get the copper

essays.stem: You must connect a new cable into an existing distribution board. Describe how you would isolate the board safely before you start.
essays.modelAnswer: I would never work on a board while it is live. First I would tell the people in the building that the power will be off and find the right isolator from the drawings. I would switch off the main switch or isolator for the board, then fit my own lock to it so that nobody can switch it back on, and fix a tag with my name, the date and the reason. I keep the key in my pocket. Next I would check my voltage tester on a known live source or a proving unit to show it works. Then I would test at the board's incoming terminals between every pair of conductors: live to neutral, live to earth and neutral to earth, and between lives where there are two. All must show no voltage. Then I check the tester again on the known source. Only after this would I take off the cover and start work, following the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Warns people and identifies the correct isolator
Switches off, fits a personal lock and keeps the key
Fixes a tag with name, date and reason
Checks the tester on a known live source or proving unit before testing
Proves dead between all conductors, then checks the tester again

essays.stem: Describe the steps to terminate an armoured cable into a gland at a metal enclosure.
essays.modelAnswer: With the enclosure isolated and proved dead, I would choose the gland that matches the cable size and fit the earth tag and locknut through the hole in the box. I would slide the shroud and the gland back nut and seal onto the cable. Using the gland maker's chart, I would measure and mark where the outer sheath and armour are to be cut. I would remove the outer sheath with a cable knife, cutting away from my body. Next I would cut part way through each armour wire with a hacksaw at the mark and bend the wires to break them off, taking care not to cut into the bedding. I would spread the armour over the cone, push on the clamping ring and tighten the gland body so the armour is gripped. Then I tighten the back nut to seal the outer sheath, slide the shroud over, connect the earth tag to the earth bar, and terminate the cores.
markingPoints: Isolates and proves dead; chooses the right gland size
Fits shroud, back nut and seal on the cable first; measures from the maker's chart
Removes the sheath safely and cuts the armour without damaging the bedding
Spreads armour over the cone and clamps it; tightens the seal
Fits the shroud, connects the earth tag and terminates the cores

essays.stem: Explain how to strip, seal and test the end of an MI cable, and why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: MI cable has copper conductors inside a copper sheath, with magnesium oxide powder as the insulation. The powder takes in moisture from the air, so the end must be sealed soon after it is stripped. I would strip the sheath back to the length needed with a suitable stripping tool, without nicking the conductors, and clean away all loose powder. Before sealing, I would test the insulation resistance between the conductors and from each conductor to the sheath, to make sure the cable is dry. I would then screw the pot square onto the sheath, fill it with the sealing compound from one side so no air is trapped, and fit the cap or disc and the sleeves on the conductors, as the maker's instructions say. After sealing I would test the insulation resistance again. The reading should stay steady and high. A reading that falls means moisture is still inside, so the end must be cut back and sealed again.
markingPoints: Explains the powder insulation takes in moisture, so the end must be sealed quickly
Strips to length without damaging the conductors and removes loose powder
Tests insulation resistance before sealing
Fits the pot square and fills with compound without air pockets; fits the cap and sleeves
Tests again after sealing; a falling reading means moisture and the end is redone

essays.stem: Describe how to make a Cat 6 patch lead with a plug wired to T568B at each end, and how to test it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would cut the cable to length and slide on the plug boots first. With a sheath stripper I would remove about 25 mm of the outer sheath without nicking the pairs. I would untwist the pairs only as far as needed and lay the wires flat in the T568B order: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown. I would trim the ends straight so the wires reach the front of the plug, with the sheath going inside the plug so the clamp can grip it. Holding the plug with the clip down, I would push the wires fully in and check through the plug that the order is right and each wire reaches the end. Then I would crimp with the data crimp tool and repeat at the other end. Finally I would test the lead with a cable tester to check the wire map, showing every wire goes pin to pin with no opens, shorts or crossed pairs.
markingPoints: Fits boots first and strips the sheath without damaging the pairs
Untwists as little as possible and lays wires in the correct T568B order
Trims square; sheath inside the plug; wires to the front of the plug
Crimps with the correct tool and checks the order before crimping
Tests with a cable tester for the wire map (opens, shorts, crossed pairs)

essays.stem: Describe how to fit a compression F-type connector to a TV coaxial cable.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the connector is the right type for the size of the coax. I cut the end square with sharp cable cutters so the cable is not crushed. Using a coax stripping tool set for this cable, I strip the jacket, the braid and the dielectric to the lengths the connector maker gives, leaving the centre conductor clean and straight. I fold the braid back over the jacket neatly and trim any loose strands, making sure that no strand touches the centre conductor, as this would short the signal. I push the connector onto the cable until the dielectric is level with the inside of the connector and the centre conductor sticks out by the length the maker states, usually only a few millimetres. I then put the connector in the compression tool and squeeze it fully. Finally I check that it is firm, pull-test it, and test for continuity and for no short between the centre and the screen.
markingPoints: Chooses the right connector and cuts the cable square without crushing it
Strips jacket, braid and dielectric to the maker's lengths with a coax stripper
Folds the braid back and makes sure no strand touches the centre conductor
Pushes the connector on to the correct depth and compresses it with the tool
Checks it is firm and tests continuity and for no short

essays.stem: Explain how to choose, fit and check a crimp lug on a large stranded conductor.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a lug that matches the cross-section of the conductor, for example 16 mm² or 25 mm², and the size of the stud or bolt it will go on. The lug material must suit the conductor, such as copper lugs for copper. I strip the insulation to the depth of the lug barrel, without cutting any strands, and twist the strands lightly so they all go in. I push the conductor fully into the barrel so that no strands are left out and the insulation sits close to the barrel. Then I use the crimp tool and die the maker gives for that lug size, and crimp in the place marked on the lug, making more than one crimp if the maker says so. I check the crimp by eye, then give the lug a firm pull test. Finally I fit heat-shrink or a sleeve over the barrel, in the right colour where needed, and bolt the lug to the stud with the right torque.
markingPoints: Matches lug to conductor size, stud size and material
Strips to the barrel depth without cutting strands; all strands in the barrel
Uses the correct tool and die for the lug size
Checks by eye and with a pull test
Sleeves the barrel and bolts to the stud at the right torque

essays.stem: Describe the dead tests you would do on a newly terminated multicore power cable before it is connected, and what the readings tell you.
essays.modelAnswer: The cable must be isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead, and disconnected from any equipment at both ends. First I would do a continuity test on each core with a low-resistance ohmmeter, linking the core to earth at the far end and measuring at the near end. A low reading shows the core is unbroken and connected at both ends, and the armour or protective conductor is tested the same way. I would also check that each core goes to the right terminal at both ends, which is a polarity check. Next I would do an insulation resistance test with an insulation tester at the voltage the Centre's tester and rules give, usually 500 V DC for 110 V and 220 V circuits. I would test between every pair of cores and between each core and earth. A high reading in megohms shows good insulation. A low reading means damage or moisture, and the fault must be found before the cable is used.
markingPoints: Cable isolated, proved dead and disconnected at both ends first
Continuity of each core and the protective conductor with a low-resistance ohmmeter
Checks each core goes to the right terminal (polarity)
Insulation resistance between all cores and to earth at the right test voltage
Explains the readings: low continuity reading is good, high insulation reading is good, low insulation means a fault

essays.stem: Explain the safety precautions you must take when stripping and terminating optical fibre cable.
essays.modelAnswer: The light in a fibre can be invisible and can still harm the eyes, so I would never look into the end of a fibre or a connector, even if I think it is not connected. Before working on a fibre I would make sure the equipment at the other end is switched off. I would wear safety glasses because tiny pieces of glass can fly when the fibre is cleaved. The off-cuts are very sharp and can go into the skin, so I would work on a dark mat to see them, pick them up with tape or tweezers and put them in a marked, sealed container. I would not eat or drink at the work bench, so no glass gets into food. Cleaning fluids such as alcohol would be kept closed and away from heat. When finished I would clean the bench and wash my hands, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Never looks into a fibre end; makes sure the far end is switched off
Wears safety glasses when cleaving
Collects off-cuts carefully into a marked, sealed container
No food or drink at the bench; washes hands afterwards
Handles cleaning fluids safely and follows the maker's instructions

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the termination of a 12-core control cable in a control panel.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the wiring diagram and the termination schedule to see which core goes to which terminal at each end, and check the cable type and size. I would check the gland size and the space in the panel, and make sure there is room for the cable to bend without going tighter than the maker allows. I would list the materials: the gland, ferrules for the cores, core markers, cable ties and labels, and list the tools, such as a sheath stripper, wire strippers, ferrule crimper and a torque screwdriver. I would make sure the panel will be isolated, locked off and proved dead, and agree the time with the supervisor. I would plan to mark every core with its number before cutting to length, so that each can be traced. Finally I would plan the tests, a continuity and insulation test, and a sheet to record the results.
markingPoints: Reads the wiring diagram and termination schedule
Checks gland size, panel space and bending radius
Lists materials (gland, ferrules, markers) and tools
Plans safe isolation and agrees timing with the supervisor
Plans core marking and the tests with a record sheet

essays.stem: Describe the checks you would make on finished cable terminations, and what you would do to finish the job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check each termination by eye. The insulation should go right up to the terminal with no bare conductor showing, and no strands left out. Each ferrule or lug should be the right size and firmly crimped, and I would give each core a gentle pull to make sure it is held. Terminal screws should be tight to the maker's torque. Every core should carry a marker that matches the drawing. Glands should be the right size, tight and sealed, with the earth tag connected and the shroud fitted. Cables should be neatly dressed and tied, with no sharp bends. Then I would do the dead tests for continuity and insulation resistance and write down the results. To finish, I would refit covers, clean out all off-cuts and sheath strips from the panel, sort waste into the right bins, return tools, and complete the job sheet with labels, test results and any problems for my supervisor.
markingPoints: Insulation to the terminal, no stray strands, correct ferrules or lugs
Pull check and terminals tight to torque; core markers match the drawing
Glands tight and sealed, earth tag connected, cables neatly dressed
Dead tests done and results recorded
Covers refitted, panel and area cleaned, job sheet completed

practical1.title: Terminate armoured cable into glands at two enclosures and test it
practical1.brief: As a group, terminate three short lengths of armoured cable between enclosures on the training board. Each length is glanded and terminated at both ends, so there are six ends: every member terminates at least one end, from fitting the gland to connecting the cores, while the others check the strip lengths against the gland maker's chart. Fit the earth tags and connect them to the earth bar, fit ferrules or lugs as needed, label the cores, and do continuity and insulation resistance tests on each cable. The board is isolated, locked off and tagged throughout, and nothing is connected to a supply. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when all ends are finished and tested and the area is clean.
materials: Three lengths of 3-core armoured cable, about 1 m each
Six outdoor-type armoured cable glands to suit the cable, with earth tags, locknuts and shrouds
Training board with two metal enclosures, terminal rails and an earth bar
Cable knife, sheath stripper, hacksaw, wire strippers, spanners
Ferrules or lugs and the correct crimp tool; core markers
Low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
Lock, tag and voltage tester with proving unit for the isolation check
photos: The board locked off and tagged, and the tester being proved before and after the dead test
A cable end marked out for sheath and armour lengths
Armour cut back, with the bedding undamaged
Armour clamped in the gland, with the earth tag fitted
The finished terminations inside each enclosure, cores marked
The continuity and insulation resistance readings on the tester
The work area cleaned, with waste sorted into bins
checklist: Took part in safe isolation: lock, tag, and tester checked before and after
Chose the right gland and fitted the shroud and back nut before stripping
Stripped the sheath safely and cut the armour without damaging the bedding
Clamped the armour and connected the earth tag to the earth bar
Terminated cores with no bare conductor showing, tight to torque, with markers
Carried out or recorded a continuity and an insulation resistance test
Used the cable knife cutting away from the body
Left the board and area clean, waste sorted, tools returned
safety: The board stays isolated, locked off and tagged; no work on live equipment
Cut away from your body with the cable knife; keep fingers clear of the blade
Wear safety glasses and gloves when cutting armour wires; the cut ends are sharp
Warn everyone before an insulation resistance test; do not touch the cable during it
Follow the tester maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Make and test data patch leads and coaxial connections
practical2.brief: As a group, make data and coax connections on the training bench. Each member makes one Cat 6 patch lead about 1 m long, with a plug wired to T568B at each end, and fits one compression F-type connector to a length of TV coax. Members take turns to test each other's leads with the cable tester and to check each coax connection for continuity and for no short between the centre and the screen. Each member's work is labelled with their name. No mains supply is used in this task. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every lead has been made and tested and the bench is clean.
materials: Cat 6 UTP cable, about 1.2 m per member, and RJ45 plugs with boots
Data crimp tool, sheath stripper and side cutters
TV coax cable, about 0.5 m per member, and compression F-type connectors
Coax stripping tool and compression tool
photos: A cable end stripped, showing the pairs undamaged
Wires laid out in the T568B order before they go into the plug
A crimped plug, showing the sheath held inside it
The cable tester showing a correct wire map for each lead
A coax end stripped to the maker's lengths, braid folded back
A finished F-type connector, and the continuity check on the meter
All finished leads laid out with name labels, bench cleaned
checklist: Fitted boots before crimping and stripped the sheath without nicking the pairs
Laid wires in the correct T568B order with very little untwisting
Crimped plugs with the sheath held inside, and the lead passed the wire map test
Stripped coax to the maker's lengths with no braid strands touching the centre
Fitted and compressed the F-type connector to the right depth
Checked coax continuity and no short between centre and screen
Used tools safely and kept the bench tidy
Put off-cuts in the bin and returned tools
safety: Keep fingers clear of the blades in the strippers and crimp tools
Wear safety glasses when cutting wires; small pieces can fly
No mains supply is connected to any lead or tester during this task
Follow the tool maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
